incident_description:
{
  "document_classification": {
    "is_summary_style": false,
    "is_full_incident_report": true,
    "contains_multiple_independent_incidents": false,
    "requires_incident_split": false,
    "recommended_output_mode": "single_incident",
    "classification_reason": "The document is a CSB case study centered on one incident at the Barton Solvents Wichita facility on July 17, 2007. It contains a structured narrative with Introduction, Incident Description, findings, hazard analysis, precautions, and recommendations. Although another Barton incident in Des Moines is briefly mentioned, the text explicitly states that the case study focuses solely on the Wichita incident."
  },
  "incidents": [
    {
      "incident_id": "incident_1",
      "is_independent_incident": true,
      "time_reference": "On July 17, 2007, at about 9 a.m.",
      "incident_summary_section": {
        "section_title": "1. Introduction",
        "text": "1. Introduction
On July 17, 2007, at about 9 a.m., an explosion and fire occurred at the Barton Solvents 
Wichita facility in Valley Center, Kansas. Eleven residents and one firefighter received 
medical treatment. The incident triggered an evacuation of Valley Center (approximately 
6,000 residents); destroyed the tank farm; and significantly interrupted Barton’s business. 
An investigation by the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) 
has concluded that the initial explosion occurred inside a vertical above-ground storage 
tank that was being filled with Varnish Makers’ and Painters’ (VM&P) naphtha. VM&P 
naphtha is a National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) Class IB flammable liquid1
 that 
can produce ignitable vapor-air mixtures inside tanks and, because of its low electrical 
conductivity, can accumulate dangerous levels of static electricity.2
The CSB is publishing this Case Study to help companies understand the hazards 
associated with static-accumulating flammable liquids that can form ignitable vapor-air 
mixtures inside storage tanks. In addition, the CSB wants to urge companies to take extra 
precautions to prevent explosions and fires like the one at Barton. This Case Study also 
examines industry Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) hazard communication practices 
and makes recommendations to ensure that MSDSs identify these hazards and outline 
appropriate precautions.
 1 Liquids most likely to form ignitable vapor-air mixtures during tank filling at ambient operating temperatures are normally those designated as Class 
IB or Class IC in NFPA 30 (flammability hazard rating of “3” in NFPA 704). In the American Petroleum Institute (API) classification system these liquids 
usually fall into the “Intermediate Vapor Pressure Products” category. A notable exception is motor gasoline, an NFPA Class IB liquid that is designated 
as a “High Vapor Pressure Product” in the API system, implying that (except at very low operating temperatures) the vapor-air mixture formed during tank 
filling rapidly becomes too rich to be ignitable. (See NFPA 30, Section 4.3 “Classification of Liquids” and NFPA 704 Chapter 6 for a detailed discussion 
of NFPA’s classification and flammability hazard rating systems. See API 2003 (2008 edition), Section 3 “Definitions” for an explanation of “High,” 
“Intermediate,” and “Low” vapor pressure product classes.
2 On October 29, 2007, fire destroyed a large portion of a Barton facility in Des Moines, Iowa. Flammable liquids and static electricity were also involved in that 
incident. Because of the incident-specific findings associated with the Wichita incident investigation, this Case Study focuses solely on the Wichita incident."
      },
      "incident_description_section": {
        "section_title": "2. Incident Description",
        "text": "2. Incident Description
The initial explosion occurred soon after the tank farm supervisor started the transfer of 
the final compartment of a tanker-trailer containing VM&P naphtha into a 15,000 gallon 
above-ground storage tank (Figure 1).
The explosion sent the VM&P tank rocketing into the air, trailing a cloud of smoke and 
fire from the burning liquid; it landed approximately 130 feet away. Witnesses heard the 
explosion and saw the fireball from several miles away. Within moments, two more tanks 
ruptured and released their contents into the rapidly escalating fire that was concentrated 
inside the earthen spill containment area surrounding the tank farm.3
 As the fire burned, 
the contents of other tanks over-pressurized or ignited, launching steel tank tops (10-12 feet 
in diameter); vent valves; pipes; and steel parts off-site and into the adjoining community. 
A tank top struck a mobile home in the community (approximately 300 feet away) and a 
pressure/vacuum valve hit a neighboring business nearly 400 feet away (Figures 2 and 3).
3 Approximately 20,000 gallons of flammable liquid were released into the spill containment. The tank farm included 43 above-ground storage tanks with 
capacities ranging from 3,000 to 20,000 gallons. Tank heights ranged from approximately 15 to 40 feet."
      },
      "other_related_sections": [
        {
          "section_title": "4. Key Findings",
          "text": "4. Key Findings
The CSB determined that several factors likely combined to produce the initial explosion: 
• The tank contained an ignitable vapor-air mixture in its head space. 
• Stop-start filling, air in the transfer piping, and sediment and water (likely present in the 
tank) caused a rapid static charge accumulation inside the VM&P naphtha tank. 
• The tank had a liquid level gauging system float with a loose linkage that likely separated 
and created a spark during filling.
• The MSDS for the VM&P naphtha involved in this incident did not adequately 
communicate the explosive hazard."
        },
        {
          "section_title": "4.1. Flammability of VM&P naphtha",
          "text": "4.1. Flammability of VM&P naphtha
The CSB tested the VM&P naphtha involved in the Barton explosion to determine if an 
ignitable vapor-air mixture could have been present inside the tank at the time of the 
explosion.6
 The results revealed that, at approximately 77˚F (25˚C) (the handling temperature 
of the VM&P naphtha at the time of the incident), the tank head space likely contained a 
readily ignitable vapor-air mixture. The energy from a static spark would have been adequate 
to ignite this vapor-air mixture.7"
        },
        {
          "section_title": "4.2. Tank Level Float Design",
          "text": "4.2. Tank Level Float Design
The design of the tank liquid level gauging system float used by Barton incorporates a loose 
linkage at the float/tape junction that can separate slightly, interrupting grounding (see Section 
4.3) and creating the potential for a spark (Figure 4).8
 The CSB concluded that turbulence and 
bubbling during the stop-start transfer pumping, in addition to creating rapid static charge 
accumulation, also likely created slack in the gauge tape connected to the float, causing the 
linkage to separate and spark.9"
        },
        {
          "section_title": "4.3. Bonding and Grounding",
          "text": "4.3. Bonding and Grounding
Bonding is the process of electrically connecting conductive objects, like tanker-trailers, to 
transfer pumps to equalize their individual electrical potentials and prevent sparking.
Grounding (earthing) means connecting a conductive object to the earth to dissipate electricity, 
like accumulated static, lightning strikes, and equipment faults, into the ground, away from 
employees/equipment and ignitable mixtures.
According to witnesses at Barton, the tanker-trailer, pump, piping, and storage tank were 
bonded and grounded at the time of the incident.10 However, published safety guidance indicates 
that bonding and grounding measures applied to typical transfer and storage operations may 
not be enough if nonconductive flammable liquids are involved. Nonconductive liquids 
accumulate static electricity and dissipate (relax) it more slowly than conductive liquids, 
and therefore require additional precautions (see Section 5)."
        },
        {
          "section_title": "4.4. Static Accumulation in the Pumped Liquid",
          "text": "4.4. Static Accumulation in the Pumped Liquid
Barton pumped the VM&P naphtha from three separate compartments in the tanker-trailer 
to the VM&P tank. Air pockets were introduced into the fill piping, and then transferred into 
the tank when the transfer hose was reconnected to the tanker-trailer after compartments 
were changed. Studies have found that static electricity accumulates rapidly during pump 
startup when nonconductive liquids are transferred to storage tanks (Walmsley, 1996). In 
this case, the static electricity accumulation was likely exacerbated by the air pockets (bubbling) and the likely presence of suspended sediment and water in the tank.11 In addition, 
the VM&P tank was approximately 30 percent filled at the time of the explosion, which 
would have produced a liquid surface potential (voltage) close to the maximum expected 
during filling."
        }
      ],
      "extraction_notes": "Single incident only. Extracted the Introduction as the best available incident summary section, the Incident Description as the main chronological event narrative, and included findings/mechanism sections most directly related to hazard evolution and consequence development. Figure captions and page headers/footers were omitted."
    }
  ]
}

accident_scenario_schema_definition:
SCHEMA DEFINITION

The output must strictly follow the provided JSON schema. Each field has a specific meaning and must be filled according to the rules below.

General Rules

Evidence

The "evidence" field must contain a short quote copied directly from the source that supports the extracted value.

If source = "incident_description":
The evidence must be copied verbatim from the incident report text.

Do not invent, paraphrase, or infer evidence.

If no supporting evidence can be found, set:
evidence = "N/A"
source = "Not specified".

Source

The "source" field indicates where the information was obtained, the allowed source are listed in each nodes.

Allowed values:

incident_description  
Information directly extracted from the incident report.


Not specified  
Used when the information cannot be determined from the incident report or reliable external knowledge sources.

Node ID

Each node must include a `node_id`, which serves as a unique identifier in the graph.

The `node_id` must follow the prefix corresponding to the node type:

- H#  → HazardConsequence nodes
- En# → Entity nodes
- C#  → Condition nodes
- Ev# → Event nodes

Where # is a sequential integer starting from 1 within each node category.

Examples:
H1, En1, C1, Ev1

Rules:
- Each node must have exactly one `node_id`.
- All `node_id` values must be unique within the output.
- The prefix must match the node's `node_type`.
- Do not invent other ID formats.
- The `node_id` is only an identifier and must not contain semantic meaning.

--------------------------------------------------
Material
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The hazardous substance involved in the accident scenario.

This refers to the chemical or material present in the process that participates in the release, dispersion, ignition, or hazard consequence.


--------------------------------------------------
Location
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The physical place or equipment where the accident-related event occurs.

This may include process units, storage tanks, pipelines, packaging areas, or other facility locations relevant to the accident.


--------------------------------------------------
Phase
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The physical phase of the material at the time of the accident.

This condition describes whether the material exists as liquid, vapor, solid, or a two-phase mixture, which can influence release behavior and hazard consequences.


--------------------------------------------------
Temperature
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The temperature condition of the material or environment during the accident scenario.

Temperature can affect vapor generation, chemical stability, and the likelihood of ignition or hazardous reactions.

--------------------------------------------------
Pressure
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The pressure condition of the material or process system during the accident scenario.

Pressure influences the containment, release rate, and phase behavior of the material.
Elevated pressure can increase the driving force for a release and accelerate discharge from equipment, while low or atmospheric pressure conditions may affect vapor formation and dispersion behavior.

--------------------------------------------------
Volatility
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The tendency of a substance to vaporize.

High volatility substances can easily form flammable or toxic vapor clouds that may contribute to explosion or dispersion hazards.


--------------------------------------------------
Combustibility
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the material is capable of burning in the presence of an ignition source.

Combustible materials can participate in fires or explosions when mixed with air and exposed to ignition.


--------------------------------------------------
ToxicSubstance
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the material has toxic properties that can cause harm to humans or the environment.

Toxic substances may produce hazardous exposure through vapor dispersion or direct contact.


--------------------------------------------------
Asphyxiant
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the substance can cause oxygen displacement or interfere with oxygen transport in the body.

Asphyxiants may lead to suffocation or oxygen deficiency hazards in confined or poorly ventilated spaces.


--------------------------------------------------
Conductivity
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The electrical conductivity property of the material.

Low conductivity liquids may accumulate static electricity during transfer operations, increasing the risk of static discharge ignition.


--------------------------------------------------
ReleaseType
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The manner in which hazardous material is released into the environment.

This condition distinguishes between instantaneous releases and continuous releases, which influence dispersion behavior and accident escalation.


--------------------------------------------------
IgnitionSource
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The source of energy that can ignite a flammable mixture.

Examples include static electricity sparks, open flames, hot surfaces, electrical equipment, or mechanical sparks.


--------------------------------------------------
Confinement
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The degree to which flammable or hazardous material is enclosed within a confined space.

High confinement can increase explosion overpressure and significantly influence explosion severity.


--------------------------------------------------
Dispersion
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The spreading of released material into the surrounding environment.

Dispersion determines how vapors, gases, or toxic substances distribute in air and whether hazardous concentrations can form.


--------------------------------------------------
MechanicalFailure
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
A physical failure of equipment that contributes to the accident.

This may include rupture, leakage, seal failure, structural failure, or malfunction of process equipment that leads to loss of containment.

If a mechanical failure clearly occurred and contributed to the accident,
but the exact failed component or exact failure mode cannot be determined
from the incident description, use "Unknown mechanical failure" as the name.

Use "Not specified" only when the incident description does not provide enough
support to identify whether a mechanical failure should be represented at all.

--------------------------------------------------
InitiatingEvent
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The first abnormal operational or physical event
that directly initiates the accident sequence
within the process system.

The initiating event may summarize closely related
operational actions and conditions that immediately
lead to the hazardous sequence.

--------------------------------------------------
IgnitionSource Special Rule
--------------------------------------------------

If ignition clearly occurred in the incident, but the exact ignition source
cannot be determined from the incident description, use
"Unknown ignition source" as the name.

Use "Not specified" only when the incident description does not provide enough
support to identify whether an ignition source should be represented at all.
